k-1.x_notes: Strengths: very concrete. Children play real games from 4, 5, 7-9 and 12 counters, the footer carries an ID, and Problem 5 (choose first or second for 7, 8, 9 and give your first move) is a real question. The math is correct. Weaknesses: the full rule paragraph is reprinted in Problems 1, 3 and 5. Problems 4 and 6 print the strategy as a procedure ('choose your reply so that exactly 3 counters remain'; 'take enough to remove 3 counters between your two turns'), which gives away the discovery the band is meant to make. Problem 3 (pile 3) is trivial. There is a lot of writing and drawing for kindergartners (record each move, 'Draw the two groups before the game'). There is no rule change and no second idea, and it is only 6 problems, which is the thin, dumbed-down K-1 page the organizer has complained about.
k-1.y_notes: Strengths: the rules are stated once, and the drawn counters suit children who cannot read well yet. The sequence is rich and correct. Piles 1-5 and 10-12: circle your winning take or cross out (3 and 12 are traps). First or second for 6-9. Traps 1-20 under {1,2} (multiples of 3) and under {1,2,3} (multiples of 4). Ben always opening with 2: he can still win only from 5, 8 and 11, which shows the greedy move is wrong. Listing every game from 4 and 5 counters (5 and 8 ways; spare rows don't give the count away). Two-pile first/second, including the non-mirror (1,4), which is a second-player win. A mirror strategy for 6+6. Misere traps (1, 4, 7, ...). Ten problems is plenty for 40 minutes. Weaknesses: the footer has no ID. The pages never say to play with counters, so the adult has to supply that. Traps up to 20 and listing every game are ambitious for kindergartners. Problem 9 gives little room to show an answer.
k-1.reason: Y gives K-1 many varied, correct problems with real thinking (traps, greedy fails, rule changes, mirror strategy) and states the rules once. X is thin, repeats the rules, and prints the 'leave a multiple of 3' strategy instead of letting children find it.

grades-2-3.x_notes: Strengths: concrete play with {1,3,4}, a clear W/L chart from 0, footer IDs, and Problem 4 has children test a strategy against every reply. The math is correct (L at 0, 2, 7, 9; from 8 take 1; from 10 take 1 or 3). Weaknesses: Problem 3 prints the whole backward-induction method ('Mark W if at least one is L; mark L if all are W'), so the investigation becomes a procedure. Problem 4 leaks the answers to Problem 3 ('a pile you marked L, such as 2 or 7'). Problems 2, 5 and 6 are tiny directed steps (build, reset, record). The labels stop near 10 to 14, so children never see the repeating pattern, and there is no rule change and no greedy idea. The rules are restated, and the table header hyphenates as 'sec-ond'.
grades-2-3.y_notes: Strengths: the rules are stated once, and the sequence has real development. It starts with {1,2} first/second for 5-10. Lee's mirror-to-3 claim from 12 is right; Mo's take-2 from 10 is wrong because it leaves 8, which shows greedy fails. Under {1,3,4}, Jo's take-3 from 10 to 7 is right and must be checked against every reply to the end; Kai's take-4 from 12 to 8 is wrong, since the partner takes 1 to 7. Children classify 1-20 (L at 2, 7, 9, 14, 16), extend the pattern to 30, 50, 61, 100 (second, take 1, take 3, second), and play {1,3,5} with a parity explanation. The two-pile examples include the non-mirror loss (4,1). Problem 8 runs backwards: find move sets that make the losing piles the multiples of 5, which requires 1-4 and allows others such as {1,2,3,4,6}. All of this matches the outline's 'test claimed strategies against every reply.' Weaknesses: there is no ID in the footer. Problems 2 and 3 are wordy for second graders. The page never explicitly prompts hands-on play. Large piles and Problem 8 will stretch some children.
grades-2-3.reason: Y gives substantial, correct problems that let children discover backward induction, test claims against every reply, extend the period-7 pattern and change the rule. X spells out the method, leaks answers, and breaks the work into small directed steps that never reach the pattern.

grades-4-5.x_notes: Strengths: play-first opening, a full 0-27 label chart, and correct math throughout. The residue argument in Problem 6 and the window argument in Problems 9-10 come close to proving periodicity. Footer IDs. Weaknesses: it is heavily scaffolded, and it prints the discoveries as procedures. Problem 5 tells children to arrange piles in groups of 7, Problem 9 hands over the 'inspect the first, second, and fourth cells' rule, and the chart is laid out in rows of 7. It repeats itself: Problem 2 reproduces the 2-3 chart, Problem 3 redoes it, and Problem 4 re-labels 14-17. Problem 6 is confusingly worded ('use piles 7 and 9 so that all three moves are possible'). Contrast is thin: only a brief {1,3,5}, and no greedy, misere or two-pile work. The rules are restated.
grades-4-5.y_notes: Strengths: concise, open problems with excellent mathematical range, all correct. It classifies 1-24 under {1,3,4}, then 100 (losing), 1000 (take 4) and 2026 (take 1 or 3). It contrasts {1,2}, {1,2,4} (same multiples of 3), {1,4} (0 or 2 mod 5) and {1,3,5} (even piles). Greedy Dana loses from 4, 5 and 8 in the first three games but always wins in {1,3,5}. Children explain why the period continues forever. Problem 6 asks for all games within 1-6 whose losing piles are the multiples of 4: {1,2,3} plus any of 5 and 6, which is a genuine completeness argument. Misere shifts the losing piles by one (1 mod 3; 1 or 3 mod 7). The two-pile {1,2} grid shades where the residues mod 3 are equal, and the two-pile {1,3,4} grid yields the unequal pairs (1,3), (1,8), (3,8), (2,7) and (4,6), quietly introducing Grundy values. Weaknesses: no footer ID. There is no explicit prompt to play with counters. It is probably more than 40 minutes of work, and Problem 5 is a hard explanation that needs the adult.
grades-4-5.reason: Y covers the whole outline (periodicity, rule changes, greedy failure, an inverse problem, misere play and sums of games) with open, correct problems. X steers fourth and fifth graders through printed procedures that give away the period-7 discovery, repeats the 2-3 chart, and offers little contrast.

overall.reason: Y is better in every band. Its math is correct and well developed, it states the rules once, and its problems leave the thinking to the children while touching every kernel of the outline. X is concrete and tidy, but it repeatedly prints the intended discovery as a procedure, leaks answers, restates the rules, and gives each band too little contrast, which a 15-minute edit cannot fix. Y needs only small edits: footer IDs and the adult adding hands-on play.
